title: Master of the rules
hook: the former barber Upali is named foremost in the discipline, and at the council he answers Kassapa's questions until the rules are recited (AN 1; Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
tomorrow: The boy who never heard "no cakes"

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sakyan princes stepped aside so their barber, Upali, could be ordained ahead of them. Your line was the barber first. Did you notice someone who usually goes unnoticed? Today the barber becomes the one the whole order turns to. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

May a monk eat after noon? Who may sleep under the same roof? What counts as taking what isn't given? In a community of people who had left home, questions like these kept coming up, and somebody had to know the answers. The texts name that somebody. In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of outstanding disciples, the Buddha calls Upali foremost among those who know the discipline. The man who once cut the princes' hair now holds the rules. Then the teacher dies, and the elders gather to recite what he taught. Before anyone recites the discourses, someone has to give them the rules. Kassapa, leading the council, turns first to the former barber.
screen: `EVERY DAY, QUESTIONS.` → `UPALI KNOWS THE ANSWERS.` → `WHO WILL RECITE THE RULES?`

segments.voice: First, the title. The Pali word is vinaya, the discipline: the monastic rule, and the training it shapes. Upali is called a vinayadhara, one who holds it. Not a lawyer looking for loopholes. A keeper, the way someone keeps a garden. Second, the council itself. The Vinaya tells it as a conversation. Kassapa asks the gathered elders for their consent, then asks Upali: where was the first of the gravest rules laid down? At Vesali, Upali says. Concerning whom? Concerning Sudinna, the son of Kalanda. On what matter? And Upali answers. Then the next rule, and the next. That's how the rules came back: one question, one answer, the whole assembly listening. Third, notice what each answer holds. Not a bare command, but a story. In the Vinaya, a rule usually comes with the story of how it was laid down: someone did something, people were troubled, and the Buddha made a rule. The rules are remembered as responses, not as commands from nowhere. Fourth, why have rules at all? In another discourse, Upali himself asks the Buddha that question. The answer lists ten reasons. Among them: for the well-being of the community, for its comfort, for the ease of those who behave well, to restrain troubles in this life and guard against those to come, and so that the teaching lasts. Several of the reasons look outward, to other people. A rule kept well is a kindness to the ones you live beside. And the barber who knew every one of them is the reason the council could recite them at all.
screen: `ONE WHO HOLDS THE DISCIPLINE.` · `QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS AT THE COUNCIL.` · `EACH RULE HAS A STORY.` · `TEN REASONS FOR A RULE.` · then, large: `THE RULES REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one rule well. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one rule you already keep. A precept, a promise, a house rule, something you never do at work. Now do what Upali's answers do. Remember its story: where it came from, and why. Then remember whom it protects. Maybe it's you. Maybe it's someone across the table. Hold that person in mind for a few breaths. You don't need to add a new rule. Just let the old one become a little warmer. The bell holds the time.
Vinaya, the discipline. What Upali, the former barber, held and answered for at the council until it was recited in full. Today's word.
Your line: the rules remembered. Today, when you keep one of your rules, say to yourself, once, who it's for. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

screen: `DAY 747 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BOY WHO NEVER HEARD "NO CAKES".`

howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries the core monastic rules are recited aloud at the regular observance-day gatherings, and Upali is remembered as the elder who recited the discipline at the first council.

fork.setup: you're Kassapa. the teacher has died, and the elders are gathered to recite what he taught. who do you ask about the rules?
options: Ananda again, since he heard so much.
fork.reveal: Kassapa turns to Upali, foremost in the discipline. the man who once cut the princes' hair answers rule by rule until the discipline is recited.

original.note: Pali vinaya: the discipline, the monastic rule. Upali is called a vinayadhara, one who holds it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strict man who loved rules.
what it means: Upali kept the discipline the way someone keeps a garden, and recited it for everyone at the council.
what a scholar hears: in the Vinaya, rules usually come with the story of how they were laid down, which is why Kassapa asks Upali where, concerning whom, and on what matter.
recall: takes the rules like a garland

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 1, Etadagga Vagga (Upali foremost among those who know the discipline)
Vinaya, Cullavagga 11 (the first council: Kassapa questions Upali on the discipline)
Anguttara Nikaya 10.31 (Upali asks why the training rules were laid down)

notes: All paraphrased; Rhys Davids and Oldenberg translated the Cullavagga (SBE 20), but nothing is quoted because the writer was not certain of the exact wording.

Confirm the Cullavagga 11 exchange: where was the first parajika laid down (Vesali), concerning whom (Sudinna, son of Kalanda), on what matter (sexual intercourse, left unnamed here as 'on what matter').
AN 10.31 (Upali): confirm the list of ten reasons and that the five named here are fairly paraphrased. 'Several of the reasons look outward' is the writer's reading of the list; check it.
'In the Vinaya, a rule usually comes with the story of how it was laid down' describes the Suttavibhanga's structure; confirm it is fair as a general statement.
The hook's sample questions (eating after noon, sleeping under one roof, taking what isn't given) are illustrations of subjects the rules cover; confirm.
howItsDone: confirm that the Patimokkha recitation on uposatha days is fairly described.
Original: विनय (vinaya); confirm Devanagari and pronunciation guide.

Editor: fixed the council order (Cullavagga 11 has Kassapa question Upali on the discipline before Ananda on the discourses; the hook and fork had Ananda first); cut 'every day' and the stock 'part worth repeating tonight'; recast the third point around rules as stories so it doesn't repeat day 738's place-and-people angle.
